Correct as stated for this context: the TCP handshake happens once per connection, which then carries any number of messages.

A server does not need a port per connection. All clients connect to the same listening port (e.g. 443); each TCP connection is identified by the pair of sockets (client IP:port, server IP:port), so one port serves any number of connections. The real per-server limits are file descriptors, memory and CPU per connection, not ports. (Ephemeral ports limit outbound connections from one client IP to one destination, a different issue.)
precise_version: Every server has a finite connection capacity (file descriptors, memory, CPU), so a WebSocket server can hold only a limited number of connections, even though they all share one listening port.

The six-connections-per-host cap is the HTTP/1.1 limit in Chrome (6 per group in Chromium's normal socket pool) and Firefox (network.http.max-persistent-connections-per-server = 6). Over HTTP/2, which most large sites use, the browser multiplexes all requests to an origin as concurrent streams on a single connection, so the cap rarely constrains modern apps. Separately, WebSockets have their own much larger limit (see L-0324).
precise_version: Over HTTP/1.1 browsers open at most about six concurrent connections per host; over HTTP/2 all requests share one multiplexed connection.

note: HTTP's guidance gives other reasons: each connection consumes server resources, many connections cause congestion, and servers may reject clients that open too many. Preventing DDoS is not the purpose: an attacker does not use a stock browser and is not bound by its limits.
precise_version: Browsers cap connections per server to be conservative with server resources and to avoid network congestion; it is not a DDoS defence.

note: Firefox's default is also 6: network.http.max-persistent-connections-per-server is 6 in current Firefox source (checked 2026-10-12), the same as Chrome's 6 per host. The value 8 applies to neither default.
precise_version: Chrome and Firefox both allow 6 concurrent HTTP/1.1 connections per host by default.

note: Correct as stated for this context.

Browsers do not count WebSockets against the six HTTP connections. Chromium keeps a separate WebSocket socket pool with a per-host limit of 255 ('WebSocket connections are long-lived, and should be treated differently'), next to the 6-per-host normal pool; Firefox has network.websocket.max-connections = 200. Opening a WebSocket leaves all six HTTP/1.1 slots for REST calls and images.
precise_version: A WebSocket is a long-lived TCP connection, but browsers track it in a separate pool (255 per host in Chrome, 200 in Firefox), so it does not use up one of the six HTTP connection slots.

note: Follows from L-0324: with HTTP/1.1 the page loads about six images at a time whether or not WebSockets are open, because Chromium and Firefox limit WebSockets in a separate pool. Over HTTP/2 all 100 image requests go as concurrent streams on one connection.
precise_version: Over HTTP/1.1 a browser fetches about six images at a time per host; open WebSockets do not reduce that, since they are counted separately.

note: True for HTTP/1.1. Over HTTP/2 the browser sends all the requests concurrently as streams on one connection, limited only by the server's advertised concurrent-stream limit.

One multiplexed WebSocket per client is common good practice (Slack's client holds one WebSocket to a gateway server), but the reason on the board does not hold: WebSockets do not consume the browser's six HTTP slots (Chromium allows 255 per host). The real costs of many sockets are server connection capacity, memory, and extra handshakes and reconnect logic.
precise_version: Good products multiplex all real-time features over one WebSocket, mainly to save server connections and reconnection complexity.

note: Instagram's internal transport for live chat and reactions is not publicly documented. The general point (one connection carrying many real-time features) is standard practice.

The advice is sound, but the stated harm (fewer parallel API calls) is not how browsers work: WebSockets live in a separate pool from HTTP connections. The cost of one socket per feature is on the server side (each user holds several long-lived connections) and in client reconnect handling.

Both options exist. For this lecture's case study, though, Slack terminates WebSocket connections on proxies (formerly HAProxy, now Envoy) in edge regions near users and forwards them to backend servers, rather than exposing those servers directly.

Opinion, generalised. Exposing edge servers directly is a legitimate option, but 'big companies publicly expose their edge servers' does not describe the case study: Slack puts Envoy proxies in front of its WebSocket servers. An interviewer's concern about attack surface is a fair trade-off to discuss, not a sign of ignorance.

The 3-5 ms per load-balancer hop is the teacher's experience. No public figure confirms it, and an in-region L4 hop is usually much cheaper. The trade-off itself (an extra hop vs a smaller attack surface) is fair.

An L7 proxy (e.g. Envoy, ALB) terminates the client connection and opens a second one to the backend. An L4 load balancer such as AWS NLB instead forwards the flow: 'Each individual TCP connection is routed to a single target for the life of the connection.' Either way, a WebSocket stays pinned to one backend.
Correct as stated for this context.

'Zero credentials' sits alongside L-0359: the edge server does hold a Kafka connection, and in a secured Kafka cluster clients authenticate (SSL/SASL) and are authorised per operation. So the principle is really least privilege (a write-only credential), not zero credentials.

Right that only a low-value credential should sit on the edge. In a secured cluster Kafka clients authenticate with SSL or SASL and read/write operations are authorised by ACLs, so give the edge a credential that can only write to one topic, and have consumers validate what they read.

A rate limiter mitigates some application-layer floods, but common DDoS attacks (UDP reflection, SYN floods) are volumetric infrastructure-layer attacks. They saturate network capacity before an application limiter sees them; AWS says mitigation needs capacity that scales faster than the flood, to filter or absorb it (cloud/CDN DDoS protection).
precise_version: With nothing sensitive on the edge server, DDoS is the main risk; rate limiting handles some request floods, while volumetric attacks need upstream DDoS protection.

The risk is real, but it is not a man-in-the-middle attack. MITM 'intercepts a communication between two systems'. A user falsely claiming membership to receive messages is broken access control (an authorisation bypass, like tampering with a parameter to read another account's data). Using the right term matters in an interview answer.
precise_version: If edge servers trust the client's membership claims, a user can claim a channel they are not in and receive its messages; this is a broken-access-control (authorisation) flaw, so membership must be checked server-side.

A Kafka connection string is not 'no secret' in a secured deployment: clients authenticate to brokers (SSL/SASL) and are authorised for read/write. If stolen, a producer credential lets an attacker inject forged messages that backend consumers may trust and persist. Keep it least-privilege (write-only to one topic) and validate messages on the consumer side.
precise_version: Edge servers should hold only a least-privilege credential (e.g. a write-only Kafka producer credential); losing it is far less damaging than losing database credentials, but it is still a secret.
